notes.subject: coverage
notes.text: All car coverage is generation 4; older cameras appear only as trekkers or spills.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: Black and white bollards with white and light-grey reflectors, orange by intersections, often with road number plates and blue side attachments.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: An excessive number of bollards, about one every 50 metres on most roads.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Most wooden poles carry a rectangular white sticker; tops are commonly a horizontal bar with uneven insulators, triangles or T shapes.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Black or dark grey sign backs, rare in Europe, often with an upside-down red triangle sticker on a black rectangle.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Town entry signs are yellow with black text and a metal frame, naming the town, municipality and county.

notes.subject: street
notes.text: Regional bus stops all feature the big yellow and green H symbol.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: One-way signs spell out Einbahnstraße in full, unique here.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Blue kilometre markers with a white border on the Autobahn, white with black border on other roads; triangular ones on small roads.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Pedestrian signs show five stripes and a figure with a belt.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: No stopping and no waiting signs often have white arrows drawn on them.

notes.subject: street
notes.text: Bright yellow mailboxes with a black logo.

notes.subject: car
notes.text: Round, usually green stickers with a 4 sit at the bottom right of almost every windscreen; yellow or red show 3 or 2.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: Letters Ä, Ö, Ü and ß; also spoken in Austria, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, East Belgium and South Tyrol.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Wind turbines are far more common than in any other European country.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: The north, especially northwest, is very flat; the centre is hilly; the far south has big mountains, though much of the south is still flat.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Area codes are grouped by first digit, and 5-digit postal codes run counter-clockwise from 0 around Saxony to 9 in northern Bavaria.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Slavic-origin endings -ow and -itz are mostly in the east; -weiler and -ach are mostly in the southern half.

notes.subject: guardrail
notes.text: B-type guardrails dominate, but A-type is common in the northwest, Rhineland-Palatinate and parts of Bavaria.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Bicycle direction signs are white with green letters; red letters in Hamburg and North Rhine-Westphalia; the southwest border state uses white on dark green.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: The real Alps are along the Austrian border in the far south.

notes.subject: vegetation
notes.text: Orange-trunked Scots pines are more common in the northeast, along with trees painted white at the base.

notes.subject: vegetation
notes.text: Vineyards are mostly in the southwest; hop fields lie in the south just north of Munich.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Brick houses are concentrated in the northwest.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Thatched roofs and rock walls are common on the North Frisian Islands, in Schleswig-Holstein and in coastal resorts in the northeast.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Black slate walls resembling fish scales are found across a large area of central regions.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Large utilitarian socialist-era apartment blocks are common throughout the former eastern half.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: Some bollards in North Rhine-Westphalia have a green top; green caps marked LVR with a coat of arms are unique to the south of that state.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: Round wooden bollards with a painted top, and simple orange posts, are found in Bavaria.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Bavaria uses white road markers split by black lines into three sections, the left showing the current road.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: Bollards standing on black disks are common across the former east; white posts with a red cap are most common in Saxony-Anhalt.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: Fully yellow posts are found in Brandenburg; yellow posts with a white plate in Saxony-Anhalt.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: Rhineland-Palatinate is the only state where bollard plates are orange instead of white.

notes.subject: vegetation
notes.text: Tiny green markers on trees are common in Brandenburg and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Round concrete poles with thicker-middled horizontal bars are almost unique to the former east.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Triangle pole tops like those in the eastern neighbours are common in the west.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Two regional Aldi chains split the country: Aldi Süd in the south, Aldi Nord in the north.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: A Slavic language appears on signs near the Polish and Czech border.

notes.subject: street
notes.text: City states each have unique bins and bus stops: Hamburg's are red with speech bubbles, Bremen's green and grey.

notes.subject: street
notes.text: Lampposts in Cologne often carry bright yellow numbers on black plastic.

notes.subject: vegetation
notes.text: Shrub and sand-covered hills are unique to the island of Sylt, with brick houses and thatch.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Many cities have signature street signs: Munich blue with an undotted decorative border, Stuttgart black without a border, Frankfurt blue with a metal border, Mainz sometimes red.

notes.subject: car
notes.text: A safari park southeast of Bielefeld has zebra-striped 4x4s, unique in Europe.
